# The Role of Transition-Metal Elements in Quasicrystals and Related Complex Phases

This paper presents research on the role of transition-metal elements in quasicrystals and related complex phases. Quasicrystals, along with their structurally related complex phases, represent a fascinating class of materials whose unusual atomic arrangements give rise to a range of distinctive physical properties. Understanding the contribution of transition-metal elements to these properties is essential for developing a more complete picture of how such materials behave.

The primary focus of this study is on how transition-metal elements influence the electronic structure of these materials. The presence of transition-metal atoms, with their partially filled d-orbitals, plays a significant part in shaping the electronic states and interactions within quasicrystalline and complex phases. By examining these effects, the work aims to clarify the underlying mechanisms that determine the electronic characteristics of these systems.

In addition to their influence on electronic structure, this research also examines the impact of transition-metal elements on transport properties. The way in which electrons move through these materials is closely linked to their electronic structure, and transition-metal elements can substantially affect properties such as electrical conductivity. Investigating these transport phenomena provides valuable insight into the connection between atomic composition, electronic behavior, and macroscopic material properties.

Several parts of this work were conducted or initiated in collaboration with Prof. T. Fujiwara, whose contributions have been instrumental in shaping the direction and development of this research.

# The Role of Transition-Metal Elements in Quasicrystals and Related Complex Phases

## Introduction

Quasicrystals and their related complex phases represent a fascinating class of materials that challenge conventional understanding of the relationship between atomic structure and physical properties. Unlike periodic crystals, quasicrystals possess long-range order without translational symmetry, giving rise to unusual electronic and transport characteristics. This paper investigates the fundamental role that transition-metal elements play in shaping the electronic structure and transport properties of these materials, with portions of the research carried out in collaboration with Prof. T. Fujiwara.

## Background and Motivation

Many of the most extensively studied quasicrystals—including well-known aluminum-based alloys—incorporate transition-metal elements as essential constituents. The presence of these elements, with their partially filled d-orbitals, introduces significant complexity into the electronic behavior of the material. Understanding how these d-states interact with the surrounding atomic framework is crucial for explaining the often counterintuitive properties observed in quasicrystalline systems, such as high electrical resistivity that increases with structural perfection, contrary to what is seen in ordinary metals.

## Electronic Structure Analysis

The study examines how transition-metal elements modify the electronic structure of quasicrystals and related complex phases. A central finding concerns the hybridization between the transition-metal d-states and the sp-states of the surrounding atoms. This hybridization plays a decisive role in shaping the electronic density of states near the Fermi level, frequently producing a pronounced depression known as a pseudogap. The formation of this pseudogap is closely tied to both the local atomic arrangements and the specific transition-metal species involved, and it has profound consequences for the stability and physical behavior of these phases.

## Transport Properties

Building on the electronic structure analysis, the work clarifies how transition-metal elements influence transport phenomena. The reduced density of states at the Fermi level, together with the effects of spectral fine structure and localization tendencies, contributes to the anomalous transport behavior characteristic of quasicrystals. These insights help explain features such as the unusually low electrical conductivity and its distinctive temperature dependence, which distinguish quasicrystals from conventional metallic alloys.

## Collaboration and Methodology

Parts of this investigation were conducted in collaboration with Prof. T. Fujiwara, whose contributions to the theoretical understanding of electronic structure in quasicrystalline materials are well established. This collaborative effort combined complementary approaches to develop a coherent picture of how transition-metal elements govern the electronic and transport properties of complex phases.

## Conclusion

The findings presented in this paper clarify the fundamental influence of transition-metal elements on the electronic structure and transport properties of quasicrystals and related complex phases. By elucidating the mechanisms through which these elements shape material behavior, the study contributes to a deeper and more unified understanding of quasicrystals and the broader family of structurally complex intermetallic phases. This understanding not only advances the theoretical framework for describing such materials but also provides guidance for interpreting experimental observations and designing systems with tailored properties.

# A Lecture in Several Parts

Prof. Anderson had always believed that complex subjects were best understood when broken into manageable pieces. On the first day of the semester, he stood before his students and explained his teaching philosophy.

"This course," he began, "will be divided into **several** distinct **parts**. Each one builds upon the last, so I encourage you not to fall behind."

The students listened attentively as **Prof.** Anderson outlined his plan. The first part would cover the historical foundations of the subject. The second part would explore the theoretical frameworks that scholars had developed over the decades. Finally, the remaining **parts** would focus on practical applications and real-world case studies.

"There are **several** reasons why I structure my lectures this way," he continued. "First, it helps organize a large amount of information. Second, it allows each of you to focus on one concept at a time. And third, it makes reviewing for exams far more straightforward."

Throughout the semester, **Prof.** Anderson kept his promise. He carefully guided the class through each of the **several parts**, pausing frequently to answer questions and clarify difficult points. By the end of the term, even the most challenging topics had become clear.

Many students later remarked that **Prof.** Anderson's method had changed the way they approached learning. By dividing knowledge into **several parts**, he had transformed an overwhelming subject into something approachable and, ultimately, enjoyable.

## Introduction

Quasicrystals represent a unique class of solids that exhibit long-range order without translational periodicity, often displaying forbidden rotational symmetries such as five-fold, eight-fold, ten-fold, or twelve-fold axes. Since their discovery by Shechtman and colleagues in 1984, understanding the electronic structure and physical properties of these materials has posed significant theoretical and experimental challenges. Among the most compelling questions is the role played by transition metals (TMs), which are common constituents of many stable quasicrystalline phases.

## The Role of Transition Metals

Transition metals such as iron, copper, manganese, cobalt, and palladium appear in a wide range of quasicrystalline alloys, including the well-studied Al-Cu-Fe, Al-Pd-Mn, and Al-Cu-Co systems. Their partially filled *d*-orbitals play a decisive role in shaping the electronic density of states, particularly through:

- **Hybridization** between transition-metal *d*-states and the *sp*-states of aluminum and other main-group elements
- The formation of a **pseudogap** near the Fermi level, which is thought to contribute to the stability and unusual transport properties of quasicrystals
- **Localized electronic states** and the interplay between structural and electronic order
